items.title: ‘Expedition 33’ Stars Explain the Biggest Differences Between Their Fan-Favorite RPG Heroes [Exclusive]
items.summary: Jennifer English and Ben Starr explained how their Clair Obscur characters are polar opposites of their Final Fantasy XVI and Baldur's Gate 3 roles.
items.content:
Maelle looking up with her rapier in-hand in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Image via Sandfall Interactive By Ryan O'Rourke & Maggie Lovitt Published Sep 1, 2026, 6:30 PM EDT Sign in to your Collider account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap After the massive year in gaming that was 2025 , few actors are riding as high as Jennifer English and Ben Starr . The pair had already proven themselves as two of the most acclaimed voices in the industry just two years prior, when the former became synonymous with the fan-favorite Shadowheart from the Game of the Year -winning Baldur's Gate 3 and the latter delivered a devastating tour de force as main character Clive Rosfield in Final Fantasy XVI . However, last year, they got the chance to join forces for a little RPG called Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the debut title from Sandfall Interactive. It quickly exploded into the breakout success of the year, also earning Game of the Year and thrusting the actors and friends into a heated Best Performance race that English ultimately won.

English and Starr were at the center of Expedition 33 's story as Maelle and Verso, the former a member of the titular doomed group sent out to defeat the paintress and end the Gommage, and the latter a mysterious, ageless stranger from beyond Lumière whom the survivors meet following a fateful encounter with Renoir ( Andy Serkis ). After the death of Gustav ( Charlie Cox ), they become the de facto main characters of the story as the expedition travels across the land to achieve their ultimate goal. Their overall importance, however, becomes even greater than first indicated when the realities of their world are fully revealed, leading up to an ending with a harrowing choice to be made between them. For English and Starr, the characters have now become arguably their most recognizable and critically lauded, which is especially notable because of how different they are from their previous starring roles .

Over the weekend, the two Expedition 33 veterans swung by Fan Expo Canada for a Q&A moderated by Collider's Maggie Lovitt , where one fan asked them to compare and contrast their respective characters. Specifically, Starr was asked to consider what Clive and Verso would love and hate about each other, while English was given the same question, but for Shadowheart and Maelle. Starr sees his duo at opposite extremes, both in how their games let players into their minds and in terms of their relationships, with one being a loner who slowly becomes a symbol of hope for the oppressed, the other being a manipulator, and both having major family issues. They're a pair he'd like to see meet because they're so different, yet also have so much to relate over, from their parents to their all-powerful siblings.

"The thing about Clive and Verso is that Clive doesn't know how to ask for help. Verso uses people for help. I think they are extremes of that. Their relationships with other people are born from different things. One is completely isolated because he's been abandoned by his family. The other does that because he's been abandoned by his family. And it's amazing how you can see those things. They could learn a lot from each other. You experience the game through Clive. You don't experience the game through Verso. Verso doesn't tell you things; Clive tells you everything . And I really love that dichotomy between those two people. I'd just love to sit down in a room and be like 'Have a chat, boys. Talk about your favorite things. Fire.'"

Your answers point to the iconic universe your values, your instincts, and your particular way of seeing the world were built for. This is where you would find your people — and your purpose.

You believe in the cause — in the idea that freedom is worth fighting for even when the odds are impossible and the empire is vast.

You understand, in the deepest part of yourself, that the journey matters as much as the destination — and that the world's beauty is worth protecting even at great cost.

You believe that love, loyalty, and doing what's right are not naive sentiments — they are the most powerful forces in any world, magical or otherwise.

You see the world clearly — its power structures, its hypocrisies, its brutal arithmetic — and you are not paralysed by that clarity. You use it.

You believe the future is worth building — that curiosity, cooperation, and the expansion of understanding are not just ideals but the most practical path forward for any civilisation.

Close Image via Sandfall Interactive Image via Sandfall Interactive Final Fantasy 16 Clive and Jill Image via Square Enix Shadowheart in Baldur's Gate 3 Image via Larian Studios window.arrayOfGalleries["article-gallery-1-769908847"] = '" Close Image via Sandfall Interactive Image via Sandfall Interactive Final Fantasy 16 Clive and Jill Image via Square Enix Shadowheart in Baldur's Gate 3 Image via Larian Studios "'; As for lessons Clive and Verso could learn from each other, Starr suggests that the dominant of Ifrit could share a thing or two about avoiding being consumed by flames. "I suppose Verso could get taught how not to get set on fire," he joked. English, meanwhile, believes it's less the characters themselves, but different goals that separate Maelle and Shadowheart. "I think the key difference between Maelle and Shadowheart is, I suppose, that Maelle's goal is to find her family ," she added. "To have this chosen family and find her place in the world. And I feel like Shadowheart is the opposite at the beginning of the game. She's forced to have these companions and actively doesn't want them."

From the very start, Maelle embraces her found family under Gustav's wing. While the Gommage in Expedition 33 only wipes away the people of the age that The Paintress brushes, she chooses to be part of the titular team despite being younger than everyone else departing Lumière. It's largely about necessity for Shadowheart, though, as a fellow victim of the mindflayers with a tadpole in her head joining the party on a search for a cure that expands into a sprawling fantasy adventure . They do share a few peculiarities, though. "But of course, their similarities... I guess both of their hair turns white, and they have some memory issues," English laughed. One thing that does unite all four, though, is that they all have problems that Starr believes could be resolved with a bit of group therapy with each other.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC.

items.title: Eagle-Eyed GTA 6 Fans Have Already Spotted A Clair Obscur Easter Egg
items.summary: Grand Theft Auto 6’s Extended Look has a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it reference to 2025’s Game of the Year.
items.content:
Eagle-Eyed GTA 6 Fans Have Already Spotted A Clair Obscur Easter Egg From TheGamer (Written by George Foster) on August 30, 2026 | OpenCritic

In a wonderful example of game respecting game, Grand Theft Auto 6 appears to have a reference to last year’s surprise standout, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

After years of waiting and an onslaught of last-minute leaks, GTA 6 finally got its long-awaited gameplay trailer earlier this week . The nearly 30-minute deep dive was crammed with a frankly overwhelming amount of details for players to spot , from new gameplay mechanics and side activities to a closer look at Jason and Lucia’s relationship .

Considering how long GTA 6 fans were able to survive off just two trailers and a bunch of screenshots , you probably won’t be surprised to learn that the Extended Look is already being analysed to hell and back . One of the most interesting discoveries I’ve seen since the trailer dropped is a very unexpected nod to one of this generation’s most beloved games.

As highlighted by Twitter user videotech and originally shared by Redditor Popular-Vehicle-8487 on the Clair Obscur subreddit, one quick shot in the Extended Look appears to pay tribute to Sandfall Entertainment’s masterpiece. The question is so unlikely that it wouldn't usually be worth dwelling on, but it is today, because one fan has created a gorgeous proof of concept video.

Earlier this week, BelmontesArt posted a clip to their YouTube channel with a self-explanatory title: "What if Pokémon had the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 battle system?" What follows is a minute-long, fan-made animation showing Decidueye, Charizard, and Greninja battling against Ultra Necrozma, complete with the Clair Obscur-isms you'd expect.

Watch On There are timing-based prompts for parrying and blocking attacks, HUD elements that pop in and out of view, a dynamic camera that zooms and sways for maximum dramatic effect, and a turn order stuck to the side of the screen. But our battle-tested Pokemon mechanics aren't forgotten about either - moves can be super effective, and Charizards X/Y Mega Evolutions are actually snuggly mapped to the X and Y buttons. Chef's kiss.

"I really like how cinematic the gameplay of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 looks, so I thought it might be a cool experiment to mix it with Pokémon," BelmontesArt wrote in the video's description. The animation was apparently made in Blender using modified character models and sound effects ripped straight from Pokemon and Clair Obscur.

While it's unlikely we'll ever see The Pokemon Company so directly pull from the parry-forward combat of Sandfall Interactive's GOTY-winning hit , there's clearly a ton of interest in the concept. The fan animation was viewed over 400,000 times on YouTube in less than a week, and it travelled just as far across multiple social media channels, too.

items.title: 'It's Incredibly Well-Made, But…' — Former PlayStation Boss Warned Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs It Would Be 'Overlooked' if They Called It a Turn-Based RPG
items.content: Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it." More like this Andy Serkis Praises Expedition 33, Says Hollywood's 'Snobbery' Towards Video Game Is Changing Yoshida, who served as PlayStation's head of indies and president of Sony Interactive Entertainment Worldwide Studios before stepping down in 2024, spoke about some key advice he gave the award-winning team during a recent lecture for indie game developers. Portions of that lecture were then reported by 4Gamer and subsequently translated by Automaton , including one piece of advice he gave to publisher Kepler Interactive while advising the team ahead of its April 2025 launch.

items.title: "It's a sad decision." Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.
items.content:
Home Interviews “It’s a sad decision.” Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.

Interviews 2026-07-29 00:01 Genki 4 Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, where the developers shared technical insights into the making of 2025’s Game of the Year. Following the event, AUTOMATON sat down with the team and took the opportunity to ask about their thoughts on physical game releases. With PlayStation set to end game disc production in 2028, the developers briefly reflected on why they insisted on releasing Expedition 33 physically despite the added challenges, and discussed why they believe physical editions remain important to video games as a medium.

Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s Japanese influences, thoughts on Unreal Engine, and studio upsizing, check out part one of this interview .

— PlayStation recently announced that it will end physical disk production in 2028. What are your thoughts on that?

Guillaume Broche: Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores. And even if nowadays, I play mainly on PC myself, we have a lot of people on the team who play on PS5 and love to collect physical discs. I think it’s part of the beauty of art too – that it’s something tangible that you can touch. I completely appreciate that people want to have their rows of DVDs and games and just feel that they own them. So I think it’s a shame. I mean, business-wise, I can understand why it may make sense, but I think in terms of the artistry of video games, it’s a sad decision.

Tom Guillermin: In our discussions with our publisher prior to the release of Expedition 33, the question of whether or not to do a physical release cropped up. A physical release adds more constraints because you have to account for the production time of the physical items, and you also earn less money per copy.

But for us, physical was something special. We also felt that the game could be special to players, and that they would want to, as Guillaume said, hold it in their hands.

So even though it made things harder and meant less money per unit, it was important for us to provide players who want to have the physical game in their hands with an option. Because that’s what we value as players too.

Guillaume Broche: To add to that, there were two very strong moments when the game released. After launch, we went to a video game store to buy our own game (laughs). Just as a gesture. And another strong memory I have is when someone from Japan sent me a picture [of our game] from a video game store – in Akihabara I think – in Japanese writing and all. I felt like a kid when I saw it. I was like “Yeah, it’s real!” It starts feeling real when you see it in stores. Alan Reynaud: Even now when I’m going to the supermarket or something, if I see our game in a store, it always makes my day. It’s a bit selfish, because it’s our game, but it always makes me go “Oh!”

Knowing that may not be possible again makes me a bit sad. And maybe it’s the child in me, but I like to go outside, buy a game, and come back home with it. It’s a nice feeling.

Alexandre Breton: And it’s not just because it’s “our game.” I think what’s cool [about physical games in general] is that a few years later, you’ll have your box, and you can hold it and look at the title and remember all the memories that are linked to the game.

Alan Reynaud: I think the same principle can apply to manga. It’s nice to read on your phone and stuff, but having a real book is just a different feeling. And I don’t think we could imagine a world where manga is just scanned and stored on your computer. It would be sad to not have it in your library. I think the same applies for games. Sure, it makes more sense business-wise, but you lose the spirit of it.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available for PC ( Steam ), PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

items.title: Expedition 33 Dev Teases "Drastic Decisions" for Next Game
items.summary: Sandfall has some interesting words to say when it comes to their next game following Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.
items.content:
One of the biggest success stories this generation is undoubtedly RPG hit, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the debut game from Sandfall Interactive.

While the studio has already confirmed that we’ll see more games in the franchise , it seems that what the developer has planned isn’t just a straight-up sequel.

On the contrary, based on what was recently said by the studio’s boss, we might be in for something different than what we’re expecting.

In a video interview , Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Guillaume Broche, mentioned they didn’t develop the RPG to please anyone, and added that some people might not like their next game, given they’re making some “drastic decisions.”

Not only that, but the developer also commented on the pressures of wanting to expand the studio, high expectations and more.

Broche mentioned (via YouTube translate), “We spent five years where, I think, overall, the dev team was just so happy to be working together. It went really well. And doing that again in our little den in Montpellier—that’s what we love. And that’s what people love, too, so why change?”

He added, “I think there’s a bit of that pressure we can put on ourselves if, psychologically, we start veering off in one direction or another—telling ourselves: we’re going to go bigger, we’re going to expand the studio because expectations are higher, so we’ll just keep growing.”

Broche also mentioned how they’re going to stick to making games that they love, and not really concerned whether their follow-up project isn’t as popular.

“And then we end up with games that, personally, I don’t play because I don’t like them. So we’re going to stick to making games that we love. If people like them, great,” Broche said, and added, “If it doesn’t, oh well. Do you already know that the next game won’t be as popular? I have no idea. I don’t really care.”

“It’s weird to say, but we didn’t make the first game to please anyone. And I think that’s why it worked. So for the next game, we’ll make some drastic decisions too, and maybe people won’t like it. That’s life. Whether people follow us or not is their decision,” Broche answered.

All in all, Broche doesn’t want the studio to be crushed under the pressure of gamers for their next project, but also admitted that if it sells zero copies (low sales), that they’ll have problems.

While Sandfall hasn’t announced what their next game is, most people — including me — assume it’ll be a follow-up to Expedition 33. We haven’t heard anything about it, but I think I can confidently predict that it won’t sell “zero” copies.

Whatever Sandfall’s next project is, you can bet a lot of people will be keeping a close eye on it, and that includes us.

Speaking of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the developers recently released a new game update that added more devs in the credits and more.

items.title: Expedition 33 director says people might hate the studio's next game and that's fine
items.summary: Sandfall Interactive isn't trying to make another GOTY
items.content:
on Google Preferred Source Google News Link copied to clipboard By Willa Rowe Published Jul 2, 2026, 1:05 PM EDT News Sandfall Interactive doesn't seem too worried about living up to GOTY expectations

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 5 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the debut game from developer Sandfall Interactive, was a smash hit in 2025 and earned numerous game of the year awards . The studio's next project, whatever it may be, might not be as popular. Director Guillaume Broche knows Clair Obscur is a tough act to follow, and he's okay if no one likes what the studio does next.

In a lengthy episode of Video Game Club on the Konbini YouTube channel, Broche discusses Sandfall's next game and says, "Maybe people won't like it. That's life." It is a surprisingly laid-back attitude toward following up one of the most beloved games in recent memory. For Broche, it isn't any different from the ethos he and the rest of the team at Sandall Interactive had while making Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . "We didn't make the first game to please anyone," he confesses, "and I think that's why it worked." Rather than pleasing an imaginary audience, Broche reveals that development on Clair Obscur was focused on satisfying the developers. They made a game that excited them. It was just an added bonus that plenty of players enjoyed the game as well.

Guillaume Broche accepts the Game of the Year award at The Game Awards 2025. Image: The Game Awards The process obviously worked, and Broche sees no reason to mess with it, despite mounting expectations brought on by the success of Clair Obscur . He admits that there is definitely pressure to make things bigger or to expand the studio because of the attention Sandfall Interactive now has for its next project. Ultimately, Broche says that this would only result in the studio making games that he doesn't actually want to play.

As for Sandfall's next project, Broche declined to share details but did reveal the team will make some drastic decisions. A big question is whether or not the studio's next game will be a sequel to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . In the interview, Broche reiterates the idea he's shared before that "Clair Obscur" is the name of the franchise and Expedition 33 is just one story the team wanted to tell. This could mean Sandfall will take an anthology approach like in Final Fantasy , with each entry introducing a new world and cast of characters. Returning to the world of Expedition 33 in a true sequel would also require Sandfall to choose a canon ending for the game, something the studio has deliberately avoided. In any case, whatever follows Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 will be worth watching.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and Windows PC.

items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Expeditioners!! Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special
items.content:
Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe?

items.title: Charlie Cox has finally played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33—a bit
items.summary: The star of Stardust and Daredevil previously admitted to not having tried the game he stars in.
items.content:
The star of Stardust and Daredevil previously admitted to not having tried the game he stars in.

(Image credit: Kepler) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter I don't expect every actor to play the videogames they're connected to, and have a lot of respect for the way Walton Goggins just straight-up said he hasn't played Fallout and won't play Fallout . Good for him. You don't want to join us down here in the pit, spending the rest of our lives trying to convince people Fallout 2 wasn't as good as the first one. Get out while you still can.

When Charlie Cox admitted he hadn't played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , even though he voices Gustave in it, that seemed fair enough to me. It's a 45-hour JRPG with a frankly quite divisive ending. You don't need that in your life while also trying to maintain Daredevil's abs.

In a more recent interview with our comrades at GamesRadar , however, Cox said he finally got around to playing it. A bit. "Not the whole thing," he added. "I haven't completed it." He's seen the impressive introductory area, though. "I've played the opening bit for a while and kind of walked around and met the people and garnered the information and all that kind of stuff. Not very well."

Cox highlighted how different Clair Obscur felt when compared to the videogames he grew up with, like Goldeneye, Mario Kart, and FIFA 98. "They weren't, like, stories that were so carefully carved out and created over the course of a game with the level of detail and the way in which information is received. It's not just all spelled out—you discover these things as you go on through the game," Cox said.

It must be an uncanny experience, playing a videogame as a character you've provided the voice for. "It didn't really feel like me... I didn't really think of it as me, I thought of it as Gustave."

J.K. Simmons hasn't played Baldur's Gate 3 or any of his games, but he loves Portal 2: 'I could have done the feature film, or the play, or whatever' Ray Chase, the voice of Cyclops in X-Men '97, has '1,000 freaking hours' in Slay the Spire and is running a 'smell build' in Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2: ' I wear perfumes and walk into battle with my fancy boy outfit' Clair Obscur is flawed on purpose, says director: 'Games that try to be perfect, that try to fix all their flaws—they're usually just really boring' Though he didn't say whether he'll go back to play more, I suspect Cox won't be collecting all the achievements any time soon. He seemed sensibly incredulous when he said, "there are people who've played it, there are people who've completed it, there are people who have 100%ed it, which—as far as I could work out—is 50-plus hours, maybe 100 hours, sometimes, of gameplay." Honestly, that is too much, and he's right to say it.

items.title: The developers of Clair Obscur gave me an interview and some advice
items.summary: We spoke about the game's finale (don't worry, there are spoiler warnings), the best Pictos, and what I can be doing better.
items.content:
Stephen Totilo Mar 27, 2026 35 3 1 Share Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Screenshot: Sandfall Interactive, captured by Game File This story, perhaps appropriately, goes on a bit longer than you might expect, past what may feel like the conclusion.

This was not by design. In my business of reporting, you can’t plan surprise endings. But it is what delightfully happened.

This story is merely an accurate account of my absurd endeavor from earlier this month, when I tried to finally play through 2025’s most acclaimed video game, the role-playing phenomenon Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , in a sudden rush.

I had a deadline: a date when I expected to have a chance to chat about Clair Obscur with some of its creators. We would perhaps discuss the game’s ending, which, in their business of making video games, they could plan for.

I will get to all of that. I will get to Thursday night, March 12, when I spoke to two of Clair Obscur’s creators, discussed the ending and got myself an in-person consultation about my characters’ builds.

It’s Sunday, March 8 and I have downloaded Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 to the portable ROG Xbox Ally X , a Switch-looking device that can run games offered via Xbox Game Pass. At this point, I have only played a little past the prologue of Clair Obscur, back on an Xbox in my house. Cloud saving has transferred my progress to the portable. In the game, our protagonist Gustave and his sort-of sister Maelle have set out on Expedition 33, the latest annual beach landing of adventurers who hope they will be the ones to take down the distant and mysterious paintress, who somehow, magically annihilates everyone of a certain age each year.

I know I’ve given myself barely enough time to play through this game ahead of Thursday, when Clair Obscur is likely to win another pile of awards at the former Game Developers Conference (now GDC Festival of Gaming) and when I’ll be backstage with an opportunity to interview the winners.

In the weeks prior, I’ve been busy writing and reporting and, in terms of actually using a controller, playing through Resident Evils .

Just back in February, I had been backstage at a different gaming awards event, where I’d met some of the makers of Clair Obscur and where I’d not spoken to them about the game, because I had other coverage goals for my chats with the winners.

For the Game Developers Choice Awards on March 12, though, I want to talk about the games. My friend urges me on. You should try to finish Clair Obscur, he says. They haven’t spoken about the ending all that much, yet it’s all the game’s fans talk about. You gotta find out what happens, he says, even if you just have to watch a video. Perish the thought.

So I’m on United Airlines flight 1777 from EWR to SFO, comfortably seated in window seat 39A. My Ally X is in my hands, and Clair Obscur is running, well before takeoff. I’ve boarded fairly early. Soon, a man with long curly hair takes the middle seat next to me. There is still plenty of elbow room for me, and I start playing. Best I can tell, the man in the middle seat soon starts a nap.

Gustave, alongside a magically powered woman named Lune, are fighting enemies called Nevrons in dramatic turn-based fights. They reunite with red-haired Maelle. As the plane takes off and begins to cross the United States, things are going well. I’m loving the combat and the look of the game’s world.

Before my plane lands, I reach the end of Clair Obscur’s first act. Big twist! I’ve been rushing, avoiding sidequests, and, wow. I did not see that coming. I’m stunned, but I don’t think anyone on the flight notices. I make sure not to disturb the curly-haired guy next to me, who I think at this point is watching a movie?

After my flight lands, I text my friend to confirm that I have not seen Clair Obscur’s wildest turn. I have not.

Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.

Much has been made of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall Interactive's production process. As you've probably heard by now, the smash hit game was produced by a studio that employs fewer than 40 people, and everyone in the game industry has a hot take about what made that possible (and often ignore the hundreds of other people listed in the game's credits ).

They've been so prolific that at a GDC Festival of Gaming talk from Sandfall chief technical officer Tom Guillermin and senior gameplay programmer Florian Torres had an entire slide advising the audience not to use their presentation as a roadmap. "This is not meant to be a tutorial or like a how-to guide on how to make games," said Guillermin. "It's a retrospective on how we made Expedition 33 ."

But let's face it, when your studio's first game is such a highly-polished hit, everyone will obviously be trying to copy your homework. Developers aiming to learn about Sandfal's process swarmed Moscone West, and let out a collective murmur of shock when Guillermin and Torres described how their small team of programmers supported such an expensive-looking game—they just used a near-vanilla version of Unreal Engine.

Related: Clair Obscur writer shares production advice that could improve your game's story

And they didn't use Unreal Engine to write lines and lines and lines of code in C++. Expedition 33 was largely made with Unreal's Blueprints system.

According to Torres, 95 percent of the game was constructed in Blueprints.

For the uninitiated, Unreal Engine's Blueprints system is a visual scripting tool that lets developers link "nodes" together to create different gameplay elements. It's used to define object-oriented objects or classes in the game engine. For laypeople, this mean it lets developers assemble game logic by stringing together nodes of scripting logic without constantly coding in C++.

On Clair Obscur , this meant that Guillermin, Torres, and the rest of the programmers could hand off content and feature development to the studio's designers and artists, allowing them to produce and test content in the game engine with fewer roadblocks that would rely on a programmer to create code.

Unreal Engine developers use Blueprints to different degrees. The system is deeply tied into Unreal Engine's natural codebase, and if you need to modify the engine in any way, the system becomes less reliable. In fact Guillermin said that Sandfall has a very "vanilla-first" approach when it comes to using Unreal. "We take all the tools that are natively present and we push them to their to their limits so we don't have to develop bespoke tools for the features and content of the of the game," he said.

Related: We're finally talking about AI, ft. David 'Rez' Graham and Luke Dicken
